title: Marguerite and the Inventory
premise: Isandro Thornbury, a night librarian who catalogs the things people almost say, is summoned by Marguerite Oyelaran, the last fluent speaker of Kavreni, a dying language of her flooded island homeland. She wants one final student before her house — and its archive of recorded voices — is sold to developers. As Isandro learns, he discovers that every Kavreni sentence carries an untranslatable final clause, and the last recording Marguerite made contains a confession she has never spoken aloud. To earn his place as her student, Isandro must translate that sentence into English, speak it back to her, and decide whether loyalty to her silence or fidelity to truth matters more — before the sale closes and the archive is scattered. In the end he translates it, she forgives neither him nor herself entirely, but the language survives in him, imperfectly, which was always the only way languages survive.
about_author: Quentin Sandoval is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent six years cataloging oral histories for a university that later lost funding for the collection. This is their second novel; the first was written entirely on the backs of discarded inventory slips.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. We meet him shelving returns at 3 a.m., keeping his private notebook of overheard half-sentences and abandoned confessions left in returned books. The city hums sleepless outside. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as diligence; he believes cataloging other people's silences protects him from having any of his own.

chapters.title: A Patron at Closing Hour
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. An elderly woman arrives minutes before dawn asking not for a book but for a student. Marguerite Oyelaran speaks a sentence no one in the building can parse. He declines; she leaves a card with a single word on it. Beat: intrigue and unease — she seems to know about his notebook.

chapters.title: The Word That Wouldn't File
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He researches the word from the card and finds Kavreni: an island language, officially extinct since the flooding, except linguists note one anomalous speaker still living. His supervisor warns against 'projects.' Beat: the first crack in his ordered life; curiosity overriding caution.

chapters.title: House on Verrazano Street
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He visits Marguerite's sagging house, full of reel-to-reel tapes, labeled jars, and a wall of index cards in two scripts. She tests him with riddles that have no answers, then agrees to teach him — one hour a night, until the house sells in spring. Beat: reluctant belonging beginning.

chapters.title: First Lessons, Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: Marguerite's chapters appear as italicized interludes. She teaches him greetings and names; he mispronounces everything. She laughs for the first time in years. Beat: tenderness; both teacher and student are being translated into each other's worlds.

chapters.title: What the Tapes Remember
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She plays recordings of her mother, her drowned village, her brother Emile. Isandro hears a language that assigns every sentence an ending-clause marking what was left unsaid. Beat: grief as pedagogy; the archive is a graveyard that still talks.

chapters.title: The Developer's Letter
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. A certified letter arrives: closing date set for April 30th. Marguerite's estranged grandnephew Theo appears, measuring rooms, friendly and mercenary. Beat: rising tension; the clock becomes visible.

chapters.title: Grammar of Refusal
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Lessons turn to verbs of refusal and apology — the hardest conjugations. Isandro asks why she never taught anyone before. She answers with a sentence whose unsaid-clause he cannot yet translate. Beat: intimacy deepening around an avoidance.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Life
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. They begin cataloging the tapes together so they can be donated rather than sold piecemeal. He finds one sealed box labeled only with a date — the night before the evacuation. Marguerite takes it out of his hands without explanation. Beat: the secret acquires weight.

chapters.title: Theo Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Theo's POV (single chapter). He genuinely loves his great-aunt but needs money and sees the archive as clutter. He offers Marguerite a care facility and a clean exit. Beat: antagonist humanized; the sale isn't villainy, just ordinary arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Sentence Without an Ending
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Marguerite plays a fragment of the sealed tape by accident — her own voice, young, mid-sentence, cut off. She shuts off the machine and ends the lesson early. Beat: dread; the reader now knows the confession lives on tape.

chapters.title: Night Class of Two
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Winter lessons continue; Isandro begins dreaming in Kavreni. She catches herself planning lessons past April, then stops herself. Beat: hope and self-protection at war inside the teacher.

chapters.title: The Librarian's Own Silence
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. His sister visits and confronts him about their father's funeral, which he skipped to work a shift. She finds his notebook and reads an entry about her. Beat: his cataloging habit exposed as cowardice; theme of loyalty vs. truth turned inward.

chapters.title: Emile's Voice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She tells the story of her brother, who stayed behind during the evacuation to save the family tapes and drowned. What she has never said: what she told him the night before, in Kavreni, that made him stay. Beat: the shape of the secret revealed without its content.

chapters.title: Breaking and Entering, Politely
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Alone in the house while Marguerite naps, he plays thirty seconds of the sealed tape. Her young voice says something he can almost parse — enough to know it concerns Emile, not enough to translate. Beat: betrayal committed; guilt enters the grammar.

chapters.title: Caught in Translation
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She knows immediately — the tape is rewound wrong. She dismisses him without anger, which is worse. Beat: lowest point; belonging revoked, the lessons suspended three weeks before closing.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Clause
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Working nights with dictionaries, recordings, and his own guilt, he reconstructs the full sentence: Marguerite had told Emile the tapes mattered more than his life — and he obeyed her. Beat: climax approaching; understanding arrives before forgiveness.

chapters.title: April Thirtieth
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Closing day. He goes to the house, stands between Theo's movers and the packed boxes, and speaks the sentence aloud in Kavreni, then translates it into English, in front of everyone. Beat: climax — truth chosen over loyalty, at the worst possible moment.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Said Back
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Silence, then fury, then exhaustion. She completes the sentence's unsaid-clause herself — the part even the tape cut off: that she had also begged him, in the same breath, to stay alive. Beat: the confession was never whole; translation requires two speakers.

chapters.title: The Sale Closes Anyway
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The house sells; the archive goes to the university, properly cataloged this time, with both names on the finding aid. Theo drives Marguerite to the facility himself. Beat: bittersweet resolution — loss proceeds, but nothing is scattered meaninglessly.

chapters.title: One Hour a Night, Still
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Marguerite, settled in the facility, resumes lessons with Isandro in its common room, one hour a night. Other residents drift in to listen. Beat: quiet repair; teaching continues past every deadline that was supposed to end it.

chapters.title: Second Speaker
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, coda. Months later, he catalogs a new acquisition for the library: a cassette labeled in Kavreni, in his own handwriting, of Marguerite introducing 'my student.' He files it under living languages. Final beat: memory kept not by preserving silence but by speaking through it; the inventory of unsaid things finally answered.
